objectives.text: Distinguish essential from nonessential amino acids.
Explain denaturation and where it happens in cooking and digestion.
Trace protein digestion from stomach to small intestine.
Name several distinct functions proteins perform in the body.
Apply the adult RDA of 0.8 g per kg body weight.

terms.gloss: The monomer of protein. Twenty kinds, differing in their side chains.
One the body cannot make, so it must come from the diet.
The link joining one amino acid to the next.
Loss of a protein's folded shape. Cooking and stomach acid both do it.
The stomach enzyme that begins chemical protein digestion, working in acid.
Judged by amino acid content together with how much is actually digested and absorbed.

questions.prompt: An essential amino acid is one that:
options: The body cannot make in enough quantity
Is required in the largest daily amounts
Is found only in animal foods
Cannot be stored by the body
questions.why: Essential is about origin, not importance or amount — the body cannot synthesise it, so the diet has to supply it.
distractorNotes: Essential refers to source, not quantity.
Plant foods supply them too.
Amino acids generally are not stored as such.

questions.prompt: Whisking egg white until it stiffens is an example of:
questions.why: The folded structure unwinds and the strands tangle. Heat and acid do the same thing by other means.
distractorNotes: No enzyme is splitting anything.
Nothing has crossed a membrane.
Bonds are not being made here.

questions.prompt: Chemical digestion of protein begins where?
questions.why: Pepsin, working in stomach acid, makes the first chemical cuts. The mouth contributes mechanical breakdown only.
distractorNotes: Chewing is mechanical; no protein enzyme acts there.
Digestion finishes there, but does not begin.
Protein is long gone before the colon.

questions.prompt: Which best shows the range of jobs proteins do?
options: Long-term energy storage in adipose tissue
questions.why: Shape determines function, and protein shapes are enormously varied — which is why one deficiency impairs many systems at once.
distractorNotes: That is fat's role.
Also fat's role.
Chylomicrons are lipoproteins doing a lipid job.

questions.prompt: The adult RDA for protein is:
options: 0.8 g per kg of body weight
8 g per kg of body weight
questions.why: It scales with body weight. A 70 kg adult needs about 56 g a day.
distractorNotes: Wrong unit — that would be roughly double.
Off by a factor of ten.
A flat figure ignores body size.

questions.prompt: A 70 kg adult's RDA for protein is closest to:
questions.why: 70 × 0.8 = 56 g. Worth doing once so the figure is yours rather than memorised.
distractorNotes: Too low — that would be about 0.37 g/kg.
Above the RDA, though not harmful.
Well above the RDA for that weight.

questions.prompt: Why does inadequate protein impair so many functions at once?
options: Protein is the body's main fuel
Protein is needed to absorb water
Protein is stored and then depleted
questions.why: Without the full set of essential amino acids, every protein-dependent function is affected — enzymes, transport, immunity, structure.
distractorNotes: Carbohydrate and fat are the main fuels.
Not protein's role.
The body keeps no true protein store.

questions.prompt: Protein quality is judged by amino acid content together with:
options: How much is digested and absorbed
The total grams in a typical serving
How long it takes to cook
questions.why: A food can carry the right amino acids and still score poorly if little of it is actually absorbed.
distractorNotes: Quantity is separate from quality.
Plant sources can score well.
Irrelevant to quality.

questions.prompt: What happens to amino acids the body does not immediately need?
options: They are recycled into other proteins
They are stored as spare protein
They are excreted from the body unused
questions.why: The body continually breaks down and rebuilds proteins, reusing amino acids. What genuinely exceeds need is largely burned or converted.
distractorNotes: There is no dedicated protein store.
Some nitrogen is excreted, but not the whole amino acid.
Amino acids do not become vitamins.

questions.prompt: Protein deficiency syndromes are a leading cause of death in:
options: Children under five in poor regions
questions.why: It is fundamentally a problem of food access. Adequate, varied food prevents it.
distractorNotes: Not the group the chapter identifies.
Excess is a different question entirely.
A varied vegetarian diet meets protein needs.

checklist: Work out your own RDA: body weight in kg times 0.8.
Add up the protein in one day of your actual eating.
Compare the two and say which way the gap runs.
Name two protein foods that would close it, and say why you picked them.
selfCheck: Did I convert pounds to kilograms before multiplying?
Did I judge quality as well as grams?
applicationPrompts.aiPolicy: These are questions for you to answer. This app does not write any part of a submission.
